title: 2nd month, Marrying the Dragon King
author: Xie Hongchou
synopsis:
Ever since I turned eighteen, I have had shameful, erotic dreams every night.

In the dreams, I am entangled day and night with a man in black robes and ink-black hair.

Granny is the last shaman in our village. She says I am the reincarnation of a deer spirit, and that in my past life I used my maiden's blood to seal an evil flood dragon in the river;
in this life I am fated to live alone, and I must never break that rule!
That year, on the second day of the second lunar month, the day the dragon raises its head, heavy snow fell from the sky.

My birth parents sold me to the man lying in a coffin who would not wake, to be his bride and bring him good luck.

On our wedding night, two drops of crimson fell on the hem of my skirt.

From then on, calamity followed without end...

chapters.title: Rest
chapters.content:
"Give it to me!"

The man's voice was as crisp and cold as ice, ringing in my ear like a bewitching incantation.

My vision was pitch black; I could not make out his features.

The thin air was overwhelmingly damp, smelling like rotten wood that had been soaked in water for years and never seen the sun.

His broad, muscular chest pressed tightly against mine, making my breathing turn ragged.

The intricate toggle buttons at my collar were undone one by one by his long fingers.

Only then did I realize I was dressed in a red satin ancient-style wedding gown, wearing a golden crown on my head, looking very much like a bride about to be married off in a television drama.

And at this moment, I was lying in a closed, narrow space. Raising my hand, I could touch the hard walls all around me, even the grain of the wood was clearly discernible.

I had a bad feeling...

It seemed to be an ancient coffin.

Yet I was actually lying inside a coffin!

That man pressing down upon me... was he human or a ghost?

He did not give me too much time to think, grabbing my hand and stopping me from fumbling around.

Our ten fingers interlocked in a gesture far too intimate...

The man's voice was low and hoarse, heavy with desire, yet the breath brushing against my ear felt steeped in frost.

"You were the one who provoked me first. I gave you a chance to run away, but now you don't have a choice..."

As he spoke these words, he lowered his head and kissed me, his arms as unbreakable as iron.

I struggled feebly, my lips roughly captured by his.

So cold...

It chilled me to the very core, making my whole body shiver.

Abruptly, the sound of fabric ripping echoed awkwardly in the confined space.

'Rrip...'

What happened next was somewhat hazy, and the world spun before my eyes.

Yet from beginning to end, he held tightly to my waist, and the world tilted along with it.

Under the violent shaking, the coffin lid was jostled open by a narrow crack, and the blinding light diluted the bizarre and seductive atmosphere just a bit.

Taking advantage of that faint sliver of light, I forced my eyes open to look at the man on top of me.

I could only see a cinnabar mole between his brows, as vividly red as oozing blood.

Set against his porcelain-white skin, it inexplicably radiated a sense of asceticism.

Fireworks burst in my brain, and everything felt so surreal.

My legs, hooked behind his waist, tightened slightly, not wanting him to vanish into thin air just like that.

My raised foot kicked against the heavy quilt, snapping me awake from the dream...

***

I sat straight up, the quilt draped over my shoulders sliding to the floor.

Barefoot, I walked to the window and yanked the curtains open.

Outside was the snow-blanketed scenery of the northern frontier. Through the ice crystals formed on the glass window, I could vaguely make out the distant white rime-covered trees and the heavy snow dancing across the sky.

A gust of cold wind slipped through the crack of the window, and I couldn't help shivering.

This dream again!

Ever since the day I turned eighteen, I've had this kind of erotic dream every single night...

The man in the dream whose face I couldn't see was more punctual than my period.

Wind or rain, he never missed a session.

Even workers get holidays, but I don't even get a day off.

When you have erotic dreams often enough, you just get used to them; by now, he no longer impacted the quality of my life.

It's just that the wear and tear on my underwear was way too fast, over the past two years, I had no idea how many pairs I had scrubbed to shreds!

I let out a heavy sigh against the frost-covered glass window, climbed back onto the warm brick bed (*kang*), took off my underwear beneath the covers, and then got up to boil some water in the kitchen.

I raised my head, and suddenly noticed an extra face in the mirror, one as withered and ancient as tree bark...

It was a skin-and-bones old woman, wearing a garish old cotton-padded jacket, her full head of silver hair pinned up on top of her head with a wooden stick. Her skin was wrinkled like the winding, twisting paths of a mountain.

She was standing right behind me, staring at me with those cloudy, whitish eyes.

"Granny, can't you make a sound when you walk? You scared me to death!" I clutched my chest and muttered in a low voice.

This old woman was none other than my grandmother, Lin Guixiang.

I had hoped to sneakily wash and hang up my underwear before Granny woke up, but I ended up waking her anyway.

After all, I was a pure maiden who hadn't even been in a relationship; having these kinds of dreams every night was shameful enough, let alone washing my underwear right in front of the old lady...

Looking from the mirror, my face was already as red as a frozen persimmon!

However, my grandmother was blind; she couldn't see.

"Did you dream of him again?" Granny's raspy voice was extremely grating.

I stammered, trying to brush it off, but Granny grabbed my arm with her withered fingers, her expression stern.

"Xiaolu, the blood of the deer spirit flows in your veins! Especially a maiden's blood; it is utterly pure, immaculate, and chaste! You must never engage in relations with any man and lose your chastity, do you hear me?"

Granny had muttered these words in my ear countless times ever since I was old enough to understand.

"I know!" I replied helplessly, turning my back to her and muttering under my breath, "I'll make sure to lock myself in a chastity belt at all times, and become an un-wanted old virgin just like you..."

"What nonsense are you babbling!" Granny's eyes didn't work, but her ears were very sharp, and she scolded me angrily, "After you finish washing up, go to the inner room and burn a stick of incense to the gods to ask for forgiveness, otherwise the gods will come down and deal with you!"

I pouted, poured away the dirty wash water, and went to the inner room to burn incense at the shrine.

The temperature in the Northeast winter was too low, and the lighter refused to catch. I tried several times to no avail, so I had to shout outside, "Granny!"

Granny shuffled over, muttered something in the Tungus language that I couldn't understand to the shrine, and that stick of incense actually lit up by itself...

I watched the white smoke rising from the tip of the incense, swirling and circling like a soaring eagle, lingering upon our household's main ridge beam for a long time without dispersing.

I thought to myself, this was definitely not a good omen!

What did Granny say before again...

White smoke circling the beams surely brings disaster!

That's right.

My grandmother wasn't just a poor rural old woman; she was also the last Tungus god-catching shaman of these ten miles and eight villages.

My hometown was in a remote mountainous area deep in the Greater Khingan Mountains of Heilongjiang Province, a place called Dragon-Guarding Village.

Don't let our village's small size fool you; this was right at the border of China, Mongolia, and Russia.

The end of the mountains was Mongolia, and following the riverbank upstream for five hundred *li* would bring you to Russia.

In winter, it was frozen for a thousand *li*; in summer, the mountains were covered in blooming purple azaleas.

When I was little, I stayed in the village to study and thought my hometown was the best place in the world.

When I went to the provincial capital for university, I finally learned what it meant to have no comparison without harm.

Here, it was covered in white snow for as long as six months.

Most of the young people in the village had gone out to work in the cities; only those mountain-guarding folk who had lived here for generations were willing to stay behind and endure this hardship.

Dragon-Guarding Village was both freezing and poor. In winter, you couldn't even eat fresh vegetables, only pickled cabbage and Chinese cabbage stored in the cellar.

Transportation was extremely inconvenient; there was no food delivery, nor was there courier service.

Mail took half a month to reach us, and we still had to take the village chief's half-cut flatbed truck to the township to pick it up.

Life was even harder; you had to go up the mountain to chop firewood and fetch water from the well.

In temperatures of minus thirty degrees Celsius, the water fetched back had to be brought inside the house, or it would freeze into solid ice in no time.

The only upside was that you didn't need air conditioning in the summer. With global warming in recent years, the highest temperature in the mountains was only twenty-five degrees Celsius.

Air conditioner salesmen coming to our place were left completely speechless, one and all.

I made up my mind: when I make a big fortune in the future, I must take Granny away from this crappy place.

Go to Harbin, buy a big house, and live in a big villa!

Until the winter when I just turned twenty, when a bizarre and eerie thing happened in the village.

***

chapters.title: Birth
chapters.content:
Deep within these mountains of ours live the descendants of the Manchu, Mongol, Hezhe, Evenki, Oroqen, and Kazakh ethnic groups.

Together, they share a belief in a mysterious religion, Shamanism.

The core belief of Shamanism is animism: the sky is the sky god, the earth is the earth god.

Animals, plants, and even ancestors can become gods.

My grandmother, Lin Guixiang, was a native Oroqen, but I am ethnically Han.

Because I was an abandoned orphan.

Granny said I was carried out of the deep mountain forests on the back of a reindeer.

She believed this was the will of the deer spirit, so she gave me my name, Lin Jianlu (Lin Seeing Deer).

When Granny found me in the woods, I was only three months old.

Wrapped in only a thin bedsheet in the dead of winter, I was dying of cold and turned purple all over. It took her a tremendous amount of effort to save my life.

Yet Granny was already fifty years old back then, and having never borne children, she couldn't produce any breast milk at all.

Those years coincided with the Northeast layoff wave; everyone was poor, and even the village chief's family couldn't afford milk powder.

I grew up drinking the milk of that mother deer, so Granny saying that the blood of the deer flowed in my veins wasn't wrong at all.

Granny had a kind heart and treated me like her own biological granddaughter, selling everything she had just to send me to school.

I received nine years of compulsory education, understood and respected these religious beliefs, but remained perpetually skeptical.

For instance, the claim that Granny herself was a "god-catching shaman."

A shaman isn't born able to communicate with deities; she had fallen gravely ill at the age of fifteen, running a high fever that wouldn't break and remaining unconscious for a full seven days and seven nights.

When she woke up again, she possessed the ability to communicate with the gods of heaven and earth and animals, and could also invite spirits to possess her body to help villagers avert disasters and solve problems.

Granny said that those who could become shamans mostly suffered from the "five afflictions and three defects" (*wu bing san que*).

Her eyes were what the heavens had taken away; after recovering from that grave illness, she could never see again.

I, on the other hand, believed Granny's brain had simply been fried during that severe illness, which was why she talked such mystical nonsense.

As for her eyes, it was most likely blindness caused by cataracts leading to neurological atrophy.

Why resort to superstitious mysticism when science could explain things?

She also claimed I was the reincarnation of the deer spirit, burdened with the destiny of enduring a tribulation.

All because in my past life, I used my blood to seal a vicious black dragon in the river.

If I lost my maidenhood in this life, it would unleash the evil dragon suppressed at the bottom of the river.

From then on, disasters would be endless and all living creatures would suffer!

Because of this, Granny wouldn't even let me date.

I seriously suspected Granny had some kind of prejudice against males, which was why she lived alone until old age and forced me to become an extinct-style nun right along with her!

In the third year of junior high, a boy in our class named Wang Shuang had a crush on me and wrote me several love letters.

I was right in the middle of preparing for the high school entrance exams and had no leisure time to bother with him, but unexpectedly, Granny found out about it.

Like a stalker, she actually followed behind that Wang Shuang every single day, blocking the door even when he went to the restroom, staring at him fixedly with those milky-white pupils of hers.

Terrified that he might do something improper to me...

That Wang Shuang was pitiful enough; whether he was scared into erectile dysfunction by my grandmother remains unknown, but his persistent spirit was truly commendable.

One rainy night, I didn't bring an umbrella, and Wang Shuang took the initiative to offer to walk me home.

Seeing that the rain wasn't going to stop anytime soon and figuring Granny's eyes weren't good, so I needed to hurry back and cook for her, I agreed.

As a result, just as we reached the entrance of the village, we saw Granny standing under a tree holding a red umbrella, still staring unblinkingly at us with those milky pupils.

Before I could even open my mouth to explain, she grabbed Wang Shuang's arm and forcefully dragged him to the dilapidated Dragon King Temple located upstream of our village.

No one knew what he saw that night; all we heard was a heart-rending scream coming from the temple.

Immediately after, Wang Shuang ran out of there in a frenzy, constantly muttering, "The Dragon King... The Dragon King has manifested!"

After running back home, he fell gravely ill and couldn't even attend the high school entrance exams.

Once he recovered, he and his family moved away from Dragon-Guarding Village and never returned.

This matter was spread far and wide. Ever since then, the folks in the surrounding villages all knew I kept my chastity, and no man ever dared to come near me again!

Until the year before last, when I was admitted to a prestigious university in Harbin.

After enrolling, the girls in my class started discussing behind the scenes during military training which department's boys were the best-looking, and which academy's boys were the most talented, but I could never join the conversation.

The sister in the bunk above me was named Tana, a Mongolian girl.

Innocent and bold, she had quite the uninhibited personality typical of prairie folk, pulling me over to loudly ask what kind of boys I was interested in.

I blushed and said I didn't know.

As if she had discovered some rare species, she pointed at me in astonishment and exclaimed, "No way, no way! What era is this, and Xiaolu, you haven't even been in a relationship yet? You're way too conservative!"

I thought to myself, not only have I never been in a relationship, I've never even held a man's hand!

Fortunately, there was another girl in our dormitory named Jiang Peiwen, who was also a lifelong solo like me. Having someone accompany me kept me from looking too out of the ordinary.

"Tsk tsk, we're all adults now. Nowadays, you can get a marriage certificate as a senior, you don't need to be this conservative, right?" Tana clicked her tongue with an air of seasoned experience.

"If you ask me, you still have to seize the chance to have a pure romance while in college. Once you step out of campus, you'll never find this kind of youthful, stirring feeling again!

Those men out in society will only talk to you about bride prices, houses, cars, how many kids to have, and firewood, rice, oil, and salt; they certainly won't talk to you about romance!"

Jiang Peiwen and I both smiled without a word, but Tana's words were deeply branded into my heart like a warning maxim.

After all, I was a normal girl too; seeing the couples walking in pairs around the university campus, I couldn't help but feel curious and envious.

Who would willingly settle for being a nun for the rest of their life from birth?

It's just that Granny had disciplined me too strictly all these years; whenever early romance was mentioned, I would think of Granny's cloudy eyes and that torrential rainy night...

Now I had finally escaped Granny's control, so wasn't it time for birds to fly high in the sky and fish to leap wide in the sea?

From then on, I would bid a complete farewell to being a lifelong solo!

Thus, on the day of my eighteenth adult coming-of-age ceremony, I made a wrong decision.

That would be the beginning of all disasters...

Tana and Jiang Peiwen chipped in to buy me a chocolate cake, with 'Happy Adulthood' written on it in jam.

Facing those few colorful candles, I silently made a wish...

I want to get into a relationship!

The moment this thought flashed through my mind, the dormitory window was blown open by a violent gale.

'Crack...'

The water glass on the desk rolled to the floor, splashing countless shards of glass.

Unfinished test papers and white paper fluttered all over the sky, looking like paper money scattered during someone's funeral...

Tana hurriedly got up to close the window, cursing under her breath, "What kind of demonic wind is this, blowing the candles out!"

Looking at the bare cake, an ominous premonition inexplicably rose in my heart.

chapters.title: Injury
chapters.content:
Tana’s birthday gift to me was a novel called *The Domineering CEO Falls in Love with Me*.

She told me to study it carefully, saying that once I finished reading it, I would grasp the secrets of dating and manage to escape singlehood soon.

I listened to her advice. Although I found the title a bit cringe-worthy, I treated it as bedtime reading to help me fall asleep.

As a result, I found the content inside to be extremely... extremely embarrassing!

On average, they kissed every two chapters and slept together every three chapters.

And the settings were different every single time...

Is this really what romance between men and women is like?

It was simply terrifying!

In the span of just a few hours, I had consumed far too much content that was inappropriate for my age.

That very night, for the first time in my life, I had an erotic dream...

Before tonight, I actually thought men and women could have babies just by sleeping under the same quilt.

Knowing is one thing, but experiencing it in practice is entirely another.

When his slender body pressed closely against me, my heart was filled with both fear and dread.

The man’s icy voice carried a heavy sense of oppression as he whispered against my earlobe, "Aren't you trying to escape singlehood? I'm granting your wish!"

I cried, screamed, scratched his back, and begged him to let me go, promising I would never do it again.

Yet his attitude was overwhelmingly domineering as he pinned both my shoulders back with a reverse grip.

"Remember this, Lin Jianlu: you are my woman! No man other than me is allowed to touch you, or else... I will make him die right before your eyes!"

Before I even had time to resist, I was shaken awake...

The night was deep and heavy, and the glaring incandescent light was on in the dorm.

Jiang Peiwen was sitting by my bed with a blanket draped over her shoulders, asking with a worried expression, "Xiaolu, what were you dreaming about just now?"

A flush of heat spread across my cheeks. I raised a hand to wipe the fine sweat from my forehead, avoiding her gaze, "N-nothing... didn't dream of anything."

"But you kept shouting, 'Don't touch me, I won't dare do it again'..." Jiang Peiwen looked a bit awkward.

And I felt even more awkward than her. I wanted to bury my head back into the quilt, only to find that my fingernails had already torn through the bedsheets.

Fortunately, everything that had happened just now was merely a nightmare.

It was all the fault of that novel Tana gave me; what absolute garbage!

Jiang Peiwen was tactful enough not to press further and went back to sleep on her top bunk.

I quickly locked that novel away in the drawer and never opened it again.

Just as I was harboring wishful thinking, believing it was just a passing erotic dream, and went about my day eating and attending classes like nothing had happened.

The very next night, I dreamed of that man again...

This time, he seemed much gentler.

His joint-knuckled, well-proportioned fingers slid down my neck and slipped inside the collar of my clothes.

The touch was freezing, yet wherever his fingertips brushed, small bursts of fire were ignited.

What followed next left me utterly ashamed and indignant, yet devoid of the fear and difficulty I had felt the first time.

Finally, he let out a long sigh, though the tone lingering near my earlobe carried a thick, possessive weight, "Xiaolu, you are mine..."

"Don't be impatient, I'll come find you soon..."

"When that time comes, no one will ever be able to separate us again!"

***

I used to be an atheist, but now those fragmented erotic dreams had forced me into becoming an ambassador for superstition.

To get rid of the faceless man in my dreams, I visited every major temple in Harbin, the Paradise Temple, Puzhao Temple, Huayan Temple...

I even specifically sought out many peach wood branches and hung them by the head of my bed according to the monks' instructions to ward off evil and ensure a peaceful sleep.

The terrifying part was that every night after I visited a temple, he would torment me even more fiercely in my dreams.

When I woke up, I would find all those peach wood branches hanging by the bed snapped in half on the floor, terrifying me so much that later on I would take a detour whenever I saw a temple or a Taoist monastery.

Soon, the semester was over, and summer vacation was approaching.

I dragged my luggage back to Dragon-Guarding Village and told my grandmother about the recurring erotic dreams I had been having.

Her expression turned extremely grim as she pulled me in front of the ancestral shrine.

She arranged nine ancient bronze mirrors, nine white snail shells dredged from the river, and nine pig bone *galahas* (knucklebones) on a deerskin rug, then began kowtowing while burning incense.

This was a shamanic method of divination to foretell good and ill fortune.

Granny muttered in the Tungus language, gathered those *galahas* in the palm of her hand, shook them gently a few times, and then cast them all out.

The moment those nine pig bone *galahas* landed on the deerskin rug, they inexplicably burst into spontaneous combustion, the flames shooting high into the air in an instant.

I hurriedly grabbed the water cup from the table and splashed it over them...

The fire was extinguished, but the *galahas* were baked into charred, pitch-black lumps, and even the roe deer skin rug had been burned through with a large hole.

Granny’s toothless mouth remained half-open, and her rough, withered-branch-like hands trembled continuously.

I couldn't help asking, "Granny, what on earth is going on?"

Instead, she pinched me, her grief-stricken tone sounding almost as if she were about to cry, "Heavenly fire has descended... It's too ominous! Why on earth did you go provoking him? He's going to get you killed!"

"Who on earth is 'he'?" I was so frightened by Granny's words that I even forgot to cry out in pain.

Granny ignored me further, packed away all the divination tools, and lit another stick of incense for the ancestral shrine.

After the ritual concluded, she rolled her pale, cloudy eyes and slowly opened her lips, "This year is the Year of the Rabbit, and next year is the Year of the Dragon. On the second day of the second lunar month... the millennium limit is approaching. Can it really no longer be sealed?"

I couldn't understand what she was talking about. Granny pulled my hand again, "Xiaolu, I've already divined it for you just now; you are destined for immense wealth and nobility! As long as you can safely get through next year, you will have smooth sailing for the rest of your life."

"Really?" I broke into a smile upon hearing this.

Yet Granny's expression was exceptionally solemn, "If you don't survive this tribulation next year, you will die!"

My smile froze at the corners of my mouth.

Either become a wealthy woman, or die...

There was less than a year left for me, so even if this heaven-sent wealth fell upon my head, I wouldn't have the life to spend it!

I was born without a father or a mother, and my path in life had been fraught with hardship; none of this was up to me.

Yet I had just fought my way through thorns and brambles to get into a key university, and before I could even enjoy a few good days, why was I suddenly going to die?

This time, I refused to accept my fate!

I told Granny that I could go without money, but I didn't want to die...

Granny spoke solemnly, "Alright, next I am going to instruct you on a few matters. You must remember them firmly. Whether you survive next year depends entirely on yourself.

First, you are not allowed to let any male of any species get close to you, not even a male dog!

Second, you must under no circumstances break the taboo.

Third, do not go near the riverbank, and stay far away from the Dragon King Temple at the village entrance!"

I nodded repeatedly without asking questions, promising her that I would definitely manage it.

Granny’s rule for divination was that one must not ask for the cause and effect; even if asked, she wouldn't speak of it.

Once she revealed the truth of certain matters, the foreseen outcome would change like a butterfly effect, and she herself would suffer divine retribution.

"What should I do if I still have erotic dreams then?" I hesitated and asked.

Granny paused for a moment, let out a slow sigh, and said, "Dreams will only disturb your mind; they cannot truly harm you. Just humor him a bit in the dreams, and remember: you must not offend him!"

It seemed Granny could do nothing about that unbridled and insatiable fellow either...

From then on, I began a year-round, rotating shift lifestyle.

Attending classes by day, going to bed at night.

In this manner, I coexisted peacefully with 'him' for over half a year.

Time flew by in the blink of an eye.

The sound of firecrackers bade farewell to the Year of the Rabbit and welcomed the Year of the Dragon.

My period of reckoning had finally arrived.

***

chapters.title: Du
chapters.content:
"Thump, thump, thump..."

The knocking on the door pulled me back from my lengthy train of thought.

Ignoring the wisps of white smoke curling around the beams right before me, I got up and ran out into the courtyard to open the door.

"Coming!"

Strangely enough, snow had been falling continuously since New Year's Eve, and it had now been snowing for nearly twenty days straight.

The snow piled outside the courtyard could reach up to a person's knees, in this ghostly weather, who on earth would be coming over?

I unlatched the door, only to find that the visitor was none other than the village chief of our Dragon-Guarding Village.

A smile was plastered across his weathered face. The chief was holding a few gift boxes, peering inside through the crack in the door, "Xiaolu, is your grandmother home?"

"She is. Chief, do you need something from my grandmother?"

I was a bit puzzled. The fifteenth day of the first lunar month had already passed; even if the chief wanted to give gifts, he shouldn't be coming this late, right?

Could it be that, seeing the second day of the second lunar month approaching, he was here to bring us some pig's head meat?

Granny heard the sound of conversation and walked out from the inner room leaning on her cane.

The moment the chief saw her, it was as if he had seen a close relative. He hurried forward and lowered his voice, "Elder Sister, something’s happened!"

Granny’s cloudy eyes rolled. "What happened?"

"Zhang’s youngest son went fishing on the river this morning and fell through an ice hole; he drowned!"

The village chief intentionally lowered his voice, clearly not wanting this matter to be heard by too many people.

After all, the first lunar month had not even ended yet, and someone had accidentally died in the village. In our eyes, this was a deeply inauspicious thing.

In fact, many feudal-minded elderly people believed that if someone died during the first lunar month, the entire year would go unluckily!

I couldn't help thinking of that stick of incense I had just offered to the ancestral shrine...

Could it be that the white smoke curling around the beams was pointing to this exact matter?

Granny asked, "Are you looking to hire me to perform the mourning ritual for the dead? My bones and joints aren't up for dancing anymore; you'd better go find someone else more capable."

The village chief shook his head. "No, that Zhang boy’s death is a bit suspicious... In short, Elder Sister, just come with me and you'll see!"

Granny pondered for a moment and agreed.

With snow falling so heavily outside, I myself was extremely reluctant to leave the house.

However, since Granny insisted on going, I had no choice but to put on my down jacket, wrap myself tightly in a scarf, and stumble along supporting her as we headed toward the Zhang family's home.

Granny often said that a shaman's duty was to dispel disasters, resolve hardships, cure illnesses, and save lives for the villagers.

Nowadays, medical care was advanced, and the villagers' living standards were gradually improving. Whenever people got sick, they would register at the clinic or township hospital, and no longer needed shamanistic witch doctors.

Yet whenever anyone sought Granny out, she would still do her utmost to help.

'Shaman' in the Tungus language means prophet or wise person.

To become a shaman, one must first be well-read in ancient and modern knowledge, possess upright character, and study many medical principles.

In truth, the reputation of shamans had been ruined by those charlatan wandering sorcerers.

A genuine shaman would not charge a single cent for treating illnesses or inspecting fortunes, nor would they feed you so-called talisman water or coal ash...

However, many of a shaman's skills had long been lost due to the passage of time, and by the time it reached Granny's generation, very little remained.

The Zhang family lived not far from us, but the snow on the road was so deep that once your legs sank in, you couldn't pull them out. A journey of just a few steps took nearly half an hour.

As soon as we crossed the courtyard gate, we heard the agonizing wails of Mother Zhang coming from inside the house.

Zhang’s youngest son was named Zhang Dezhu, four years older than me. If I remembered correctly, he seemed to have been born in the Year of the Dragon.

His corpse was currently laid out in the living room, his skin turned pale and greenish-blue from being soaked, his cotton-padded clothes completely saturated with water, and the tips of his hair frozen into icicles.

"Dezhu must have run into some evil entity. Early this morning, he insisted on eating river fish, and before dawn he ran out holding a fishing rod and an ice pick. My parents tried to stop him for ages, but couldn't..."

Zhang Dezhu's older brother, Dehai, leaned against the doorframe smoking a cigarette, saying heavily, "He was nowhere to be seen all morning, and then he ended up like this!"

Granny leaned her head toward me, gesturing for me to describe the deceased's condition.

Judging purely from his outward appearance, I really couldn't tell how Zhang Dezhu differed from any other drowning victims.

After all, it was winter; no matter how good a swimmer's skills were, if they accidentally fell through an ice hole, the survival rate was slim.

Even if he could withstand the bone-chilling temperature underwater, it would be extremely difficult for him to muster the physical strength to crawl back onto the ice surface.

Just as I was about to speak, Mother Zhang walked out from the inner room with tear-stained cheeks, clutching a red belt in her hand.

"My son's death is definitely not as simple as accidentally falling into the water! When he was a little boy, his throat was pierced by a fishbone while eating river fish, and from then on he never touched a single bite of fish again. How could he suddenly propose eating fish?" Mother Zhang wiped away the tears from the corners of her eyes, speaking sternly.

"Before he left, he even insisted on taking off the red belt tied for his zodiac birth year, acting as if he were possessed by a demon!"

Mother Zhang cursed bitterly, "My son must have been dragged down as a substitute by a water ghost! Don't let me find out whose family's ghost it is, or I'll dig up their ancestral graves for eight generations!"

The corners of my mouth twitched.

I hadn't heard the term 'dragging down a substitute' for many years.

When I was little, the old folks in the village always said that those who drowned in the river were taken by the Dragon King to be his little soldiers, and they could never enter the cycle of reincarnation.

Those wandering ghosts also wanted to be human again, so every summer when the river tide rose, someone would inevitably fall in.

Those people were dragged down as substitutes by water ghosts, taking their place to serve before the Dragon King so that the ghost could float off to the netherworld and be reincarnated.

I had always believed these were just ghost stories made up by the village elders to scare children away from getting close to the river during high tides.

I never expected Mother Zhang to actually believe it!

Granny didn't speak. Instead, she walked up to Zhang Dezhu's corpse and reached out to touch his brow bone. "Who pulled him out of the river?"

"Nobody pulled him out." The village chief's expression was somewhat peculiar. "His body was personally sent back by the Dragon King!"

As soon as these words were spoken, the atmosphere in the room turned deeply eerie.

Zhang Dehai was the first to break the silence. "Dezhu hadn't come back all morning. As it was getting close to lunchtime, my mom told me to go look for him. I walked all the way along the riverbank, but with this blinding snowy weather, there wasn't even a single human shadow by the river.

When I walked past that Dragon King Temple at the entrance of the village, I saw a large ice hole broken on the surface of the river. Dezhu's fishing rod was still sitting there on the ice, but he was gone.

At that moment, I thought to myself: *Oh no, Dezhu must have fallen in!*

I hurriedly ran onto the river surface, but right then, I suddenly heard Dezhu's voice coming from not far away, calling out in a very weak tone:

*'Brother, I'm right here...'*

I followed the sound and found that I had arrived at the Dragon King Temple. Lying stiffly on the ground right at the temple entrance was a person.

When I went closer to look, it actually turned out to be Dezhu!

The water on his body had frozen into ice, and a thin layer of snow was dusted over him. Clearly, he had been dead for at least two hours..."

Hearing this, I felt a gust of cold wind crawl down my spine, and I subconsciously edged closer to Granny.

If Zhang Dezhu had already been dead for a long time, then who on earth was the person by the riverbank calling out to Zhang Dehai as 'brother'?

chapters.title: Scenery
chapters.content:
Granny's clouded white eyes rolled slightly, and her voice was hoarse. "Are you sure you found this boy at the entrance of the Dragon King Temple?"

Zhang Dehai was briefly taken aback. "I'm sure! I heard it clearly from the river. That voice definitely came from inside the Dragon King Temple!"

When he finished speaking, everyone in the room fell silent again.

The reason was simple: there was something unsettling about that Dragon King Temple...

Our village has stood along the river for generations. According to the latest archaeological findings, there were already traces of human activity here two thousand years ago.

The river that flows past Dragon-Guarding Village is the Heilongjiang River.

The Heilongjiang rises in Ergun, runs through China, Mongolia and Russia, and was known in ancient times as the Yu River, the Black Water, and other names.

A local gazetteer once recorded that the waters of the Heilongjiang are black and wind like a flood dragon, hence its name, "Black Dragon River."

But the old people in the village tell a different story, passed down by word of mouth.

The legend goes that in remote antiquity, an evil flood dragon with a jet-black body lived in the river and delighted in eating children under the age of ten.

Every year, the people along the riverbank had to choose two pairs of boys and girls as offerings to the evil dragon. Otherwise it would stir up storms and send floods sweeping through the villages, leaving the people on both banks with no means to live.

As time went on, the young people of the village fled one by one. People turned pale at the mention of the river, and children were too frightened even to cry at night.

The shamans performed a ritual and summoned a little white dragon. Moved by the people's suffering, it fought the black dragon to the death. After seven days and seven nights of battle, neither side could gain the upper hand.

The villagers took up their hoes and sickles and rushed forward to help the white dragon.

In the end, working together, they defeated the black dragon, and from then on the weather was mild and the harvests were bountiful.

The black dragon plunged into the river, and its blood dyed the water a murky black. That is how the Heilongjiang got its name.

To commemorate the white dragon, the people built a Dragon King Temple upstream. Any fisherman heading out on the water must first go to the temple to burn incense and pray for the safe return of everyone on the boat.

Granny, however, said this story was fine for listening but should not be taken at face value.

I asked her what the truth was. Was the dragon guarded by Dragon-Guarding Village that little white dragon?

From the sound of it, he must be one of the good guys, right?

Granny didn't want to explain. Instead, she looked at me with a pitying expression.

She said that sooner or later, I would find out for myself.

But she hoped that day would never come...

As for why I say there is something unsettling about the Dragon King Temple, it is because of the flood of '98, when Dragon-Guarding Village was the hardest-hit area.

I hadn't been born yet, but Granny told me that every house in our village was washed away, the carcasses of wild animals and livestock floated on the river, and even big trees were torn up by the roots and lay across the water.

Fortunately, the village chief had foresight and led the entire village to safety in town ahead of time, so no one was hurt or killed.

On the day the villagers left by truck, they all saw with their own eyes the tragic sight of the floodwaters swallowing their homes.

When the surge reached the Dragon King Temple at the village entrance, it actually split into two on its own and flowed around the temple gate toward other places.

Amid the raging river and the ruins everywhere, only the Dragon King Temple remained standing firmly in place, unshaken.

When the flood receded and everyone returned to Dragon-Guarding Village to rebuild their homes, someone discovered that a coffin had appeared inside the Dragon King Temple out of nowhere.

The coffin was shaped like a little boat with two pointed ends, not a burial style commonly seen in the Central Plains.

Two dragons playing with a pearl were carved on the red lid, the craftsmanship so exquisite that even the dragons' scales looked lifelike.

Scenes from the Battle of Zhulu were painted on the prow and stern, and a line of scribbles that no one could read was carved into the lower right corner.

The wood used for the coffin was also very special. Granny said it was called red toon sunken wood.

Because it had been soaked in water for so long, the red pigment in the wood had gradually seeped out, leaving it bright red like blood.

This boat-shaped coffin must have lain at the bottom of the river for quite some years, and was washed up by the flood this time.

Back then, few people in our village had much education. The county sent scholars to investigate, and they said the scribbles carved on the coffin lid were the oldest writing in China, oracle bone script.

The general meaning of that line was: Dragon-Suppressing Coffin.

The scholars couldn't tell the exact age of the coffin either, but judging by the style of the painted beams inside the Dragon King Temple, they concluded that the temple and the Dragon-Suppressing Coffin belonged to the same period. Beyond that, nothing could be known.

One of them patted the coffin lid and said it seemed to be empty inside.

He put his ear close to listen, and his face suddenly changed color. He let out a cry and stumbled backward.

The villagers asked curiously what he had heard.

He said in terror, "I... I think I heard a human heartbeat!"

How could that be?

Only the living have heartbeats.

But how could a living person be sealed in a coffin?

"Maybe I just heard wrong..."

Even he found it deeply eerie and tried to brush it off, yet he would not go near the Dragon-Suppressing Coffin again for anything.

He planned to go back first and report to the municipal bureau, so the province could send people to take a look.

But halfway back to the county, the scholar was in a car accident. The car, with him in it, was hit and driven into the river, and even after several days of dragging, no trace of him was found.

Judging by the river's current at the time, he had probably been swept all the way to Russia. His chances of survival were slim to none.

All of this was experienced firsthand by every villager. I'm not making it up.

From then on, everyone kept well away from the Dragon King Temple at the village entrance. Even a strapping man of six feet would not dare walk past its gate, let alone swim or fish anywhere nearby.

Zhang Dehai said Zhang Dezhu's body was lying inside the Dragon King Temple. Even the village chief, who was always the one to take charge, knitted his brows and said nothing, a cigarette dangling from his lips.

Granny asked again, "When you saw Dezhu, was there anything strange about him?"

Zhang Dehai thought carefully. "Nothing strange, really. It's just that he was clutching a river mussel in his palm..."

"Bring me that mussel!" Granny said.

Zhang Dehai handed the mussel to Granny. I tilted my head to look and saw that it was just an ordinary chum salmon mussel from the river.

Granny told me to go and pick up some small stones.

I knew she wanted to question it. I collected nine pebbles from the snow in the yard and arranged them in a circle, then placed the palm-sized mussel at the center of the formation.

She muttered words under her breath. As her tone grew higher and higher, the mussel on the ground actually began to tremble violently, making a clattering sound.

After two minutes, the shell cracked.

A pool of thick, pitch-black liquid oozed out, like the ink squirted by a cuttlefish...

Granny's expression was grim in the extreme, and her forehead was covered in cold sweat. "He has come back... He is about to return!"

"Who is about to return?" the village chief pressed.

Granny's toothless lips quivered, and she slowly spat out two words: "The Dragon King!"

Everyone present sucked in a cold breath, clearly terrified of those two words.

Granny said solemnly, "Dezhu's body must be buried as soon as possible, or there will be disaster!"

Mother Zhang was displeased at once. "My son's seventh day hasn't even passed yet, so we can't bury him! Besides, the snow outside is so thick and the ground is frozen solid. How are we supposed to dig?"

The people in our village are old-fashioned, and the elders refuse to accept cremation, wanting to be buried in the earth to rest in peace.

Luckily, every household has its own farmland, and people are simply buried in their own fields after death, so no one interferes.

The village chief also thought burying him now was too hasty. "Elder Sister," he said earnestly, "the first lunar month isn't even over yet. Holding a funeral now is probably inauspicious!"

Granny gave a cold laugh. "By the time the seventh day really passes, it will all be too late! If you won't listen to this old woman, then do as you please."

"Xiaolu, let's go!"

I helped Granny up and, in front of the Zhang family and the whole village, turned and walked away.

Granny's divinations had never once been wrong, and that very night, something happened at the Zhang house.

chapters.title: Death
chapters.content:
The sky had barely begun to lighten and I was still lying on the heated brick bed catching up on sleep when the big iron gate outside the yard was slapped so hard it rang.

Full of resentment, I went to open it, only to find Zhang Dehai with a flushed face, panting as if he'd seen a ghost. "Where's Granny Lin? Something... something terrible has happened!"

As if she had expected this all along, Granny calmly came out of the house leaning on her cane and asked offhandedly, "Is it a bad one?"

Zhang Dehai answered awkwardly, "It went on all night. No one in my family slept a wink."

Granny said nothing more. She held out her hand, signaling me to help her walk to the Zhang house.

Only on the way did I learn that last night, everyone in the Zhang family had heard Zhang Dezhu crying.

"It's so cold in the water, wuwu... I'm freezing to death!"

The voice seemed to come from right outside the window. Zhang Dehai took a flashlight out to look, but saw nothing.

At first it was only soft whimpering, but later it turned into deafening wails.

"It's so cold, I can't stand it anymore!"

Mother Zhang couldn't bear to listen. She dug out a quilt and covered Zhang Dezhu's body with it, saying tearfully, "My child, Mom knows you're cold. Tomorrow Mom will burn you some new clothes, and soon you won't be cold anymore..."

Strangely, once the quilt was in place, the crying really did stop.

But after being stirred up like that, the Zhang family couldn't sleep either. They simply gathered in the living room and sat guard beside Zhang Dezhu's body, not daring to close their eyes for the entire night.

After hearing this I asked in confusion, "By that logic, isn't the problem already solved? Can't you just burn some clothes for Zhang Dezhu today?"

Zhang Dehai hesitated. "You'll know when you go in and see."

As he spoke, we had already reached the Zhang family's courtyard.

I walked up to Zhang Dezhu's body, steeled my nerves, and lifted the thick quilt. The sight before me nearly made me throw up last night's dinner...

Zhang Dezhu, lying on the concrete floor, looked as if he had been soaked in water for a very long time. The skin all over his body was shriveled and deathly pale, like a crumpled ball of paper.

His eyeballs, however, bulged out unnaturally, so far that even his eyelids couldn't cover them. His eyes glared like two bronze bells, as if he had died with a grievance.

"What did you do to him? How... how could he end up like this!" I clapped a hand over my mouth and gasped.

I finally understood why the police hate handling cases of bodies dumped in water. The sight was not something an ordinary person could bear.

Mother Zhang's attitude was clearly much better than the day before, and she explained anxiously, "I thought that if I changed Dezhu out of those wet clothes, maybe he wouldn't be cold anymore. But the moment I finished undressing him, Dezhu's body turned into this..."

I was completely baffled.

Zhang Dezhu had been in the water for a few hours at most. His body shouldn't have been soaked to this degree!

And he had been perfectly fine during the day, so how had he shriveled into a dried corpse overnight!

Granny was unmoved by our shock and let out a soft snort. "If you insist on keeping him for two more days, the body will only rot worse, and in the end there will be nothing left but a skeleton!"

Zhang Dehai hurried forward to apologize. "Granny Lin, it was my mother's fault yesterday. We're old neighbors, so please don't hold it against her! We'll go and prepare the coffin right now. We'll bury him wherever you say!"

"Before dark, find a sunny slope as soon as you can and bury him with his head pointing toward the Heilongjiang. Remember, no one may cry during the funeral procession!" Granny said sternly.

Zhang Dehai froze for a moment.

The demand was rather unreasonable. The one who had died was their own flesh and blood, and they weren't even allowed to let out a single wail!

After hesitating for half a minute, he nodded in agreement anyway.

Mother Zhang was reluctant, but she was clearly worn out by Zhang Dezhu's antics too.

Her expression was vague and unsettled. She sat dazedly on the edge of the heated bed, looking at Zhang Dehai, and did not object.

There was still some time before dark, so the Zhang family immediately set about preparing what was needed for the burial.

It was the Lunar New Year, and the shopkeepers in the village who sold funeral goods didn't want to touch such bad luck either. In the end, it took ten times the usual price to get the owner to rush out some paper ingots and spirit money.

We had a simple lunch at the Zhang house, and then everyone hurried to send Zhang Dezhu on his way.

Zhang Dehai, at the head, carried the white soul-summoning banner, relatives helped scatter paper money, and several tough-fated strongmen had been hired at a high price to carry the coffin.

Mother Zhang walked at the very back of the procession.

Mother Zhang's face showed the utmost grief, yet she forced herself not to cry out.

Apart from the howling wind and the crunch of shoes on the snow, the group walked toward the hillside like actors in a pantomime.

As I passed by Mother Zhang, I happened to glance at the photo frame she was holding in her arms.

The person in the black-and-white photograph was staring straight back at me, the corners of his mouth lifted in a smile both eerie and charming.

My scalp went numb, and I stood rooted to the spot.

The face in that photograph... was mine!

"Xiaolu, Xiaolu..."

Granny called out several times before I finally came back to myself.

I looked again carefully and saw that the photo in the frame had turned back into Zhang Dezhu.

Could I have seen wrong?

I helped Granny to the chosen grave site and watched the men dig, shovelful after shovelful.

My mind kept replaying that black-and-white photograph, and I was still shaken.

Once the grave was dug, Zhang Dezhu was placed in the coffin with his head toward the river and his feet toward the snow mountain.

Just as they were about to close the lid and drive in the nails, Mother Zhang could hold back no longer. She threw herself down in front of the coffin and let out a wail.

"My child, how could you leave just like this? How am I supposed to go on living!"

"You mustn't cry!" Granny barked.

But it was already too late...

The moment Mother Zhang cried out, Zhang Dezhu's body began to rot at a speed visible to the naked eye. The corpse spots on his skin turned green, muddy water flowed from his nose and mouth, and his abdomen gradually swelled.

Even in the dead of winter, a pungent stench of decay drifted out of the coffin.

The helpers the Zhang family had hired all covered their noses and mouths and muttered, "It stinks!"

I was badly overcome by the smell too. Only Granny stayed calm, shouting at them, "Hurry up and close the lid!"

The men scrambled to close the coffin lid and then threw earth over it, shovelful after shovelful.

Only when the yellow earth had piled into a small mound and the coffin could no longer be seen did everyone breathe a sigh of relief.

Granny's expression was still stern. She glared at Mother Zhang with her pale pupils. "You just broke the rules. I'm afraid this isn't over!"

With that, paying no attention to the Zhang family's faces, she dragged me toward home.

Back in the room, I immediately heated water and took a bath, washing all the clothes that had picked up the smell of the corpse.

When I came out of the bathroom, I found Granny kneeling before the shrine, burning incense.

I crept over on tiptoe and heard her murmuring softly.

"Spirit, I did wrong and brought about the death of that Zhang boy. Whatever punishment there is, let it fall on me. Don't make things hard for Xiaolu. She knows nothing..."

My mind reeled as if struck by lightning.

What had Granny done wrong?

Could Zhang Dezhu's death have something to do with Granny?

Before I could come to my senses, the familiar sound of knocking came from outside the door again.

chapters.title: Shock
chapters.content:
This time I really couldn’t keep it together. The man had already been buried; how much longer was the Zhang family going to torment my grandmother?!

Was there no end to this?!

Furious, I ran over to open the door, fully intending to unleash a string of vicious curses. But the person standing outside wasn’t Zhang Dehai; it was the village chief.

"Xiaolu, my daughter-in-law went into premature labor! Hurry and get your grandmother to come help!" The village chief stomped his feet, his face etched with anxiety.

I remembered that the village chief's young wife was only just past her eighth month of pregnancy. Why had she suddenly gone into premature labor?

This situation was getting a bit tricky...

The doctors at the village clinic had all gone back to town for the New Year. The snow on the roads was too thick right now; even walking was a struggle, and cars simply couldn't move.

By the time the village chief went to town to fetch a doctor, the baby would probably already be born.

No wonder he was so desperate he'd turn to any doctor he could find, coming all the way to my grandmother's place!

Only... my grandmother had never raised children of her own. Did she actually know how to deliver a baby?

While I hesitated, Granny had already felt her way out of the room, leaning against the wall.

The dim night light made Granny's expression look inexplicably haggard, her posture much more hunched than usual, as if her soul had been sucked dry by some demon or monster.

"Let's go," she parted her lips, her voice as weak as a mosquito's hum.

I hurriedly stepped forward to support her, a vague sense of dread washing over me. "Granny, were you overworked today?"

Granny shook her head, gently pushed my hand away, and instructed, "Do not step out of this courtyard tonight. Stay obediently inside your room, and no matter what you hear, you are not allowed to open the door!"

I froze. Connecting this to what had happened during the day, I figured Granny must have her reasons for saying this, so I obediently nodded. "Okay."

After Granny and the village chief left, I locked the front gate again, even giving it a shake to make sure it was securely fastened before returning to my bedroom.

It was nine-thirty at night. I dug out a college physics textbook to use as a sleep aid, and sure enough, as I read, I drifted off to sleep...

I didn't know how long I had been asleep when I vaguely heard someone knocking on the door outside.

*Thud, thud, thud...*

Thinking Granny had returned from delivering the baby, I rubbed my eyes and climbed out of bed, still half-asleep.

Just as I reached the courtyard, I suddenly remembered what Granny had said before she left...

*No matter what you hear, you are not allowed to open the door...*

All my sleepiness vanished instantly. I didn't dare get any closer, casting a wary look at the heavy iron gate of our house.

At that moment, a familiar voice drifted from outside the door, "Xiaolu, open the door for Granny!"

Hearing that, every hair on my body stood on end.

When Granny left, I had clearly seen her pick up the key from the windowsill and slip it into her pocket.

Blind as she was, she was already used to living in darkness, and fumbling to open a door with a key was well within her abilities.

So the person behind that door definitely wasn't my grandmother!

"Xiaolu, how can your heart be so cruel? It's so cold outside, are you trying to freeze Granny to death?"

That hoarse voice gradually grew deeper and richer, the heavy resentment in its tone palpable even through the door.

"You ungrateful wretch, have you forgotten who carried you back from the woods? If it weren't for me, you would have frozen to death long ago..."

By the end, the voice had completely transformed into that of a rough, burly man; there was no trace of Granny left at all!

Terrified, I turned and bolted, diving back under the covers of my bed.

The knocking continued. The thing outside, man or ghost, clearly losing its patience, began pounding on the door with growing violence.

The initial gentle *thud-thud* escalated into a deafening *bang-bang*, each strike making my heart leap into my throat.

I buried myself deep inside the quilt, trying to use the blanket as a barrier to shut out those terrifying noises.

Gradually, the knocking really did stop.

I cautiously poked my head out, listening intently for two full minutes.

Aside from the rustling sound of wind and snow outside the window, there was nothing else.

Had that thing really left?

Just as I was harboring doubts and preparing to climb out of bed to check the window, I realized I couldn't move!

My hands and feet were nailed firmly to the *kang* [1], as if refusing to obey my commands; I couldn't even manage the simple task of throwing off the quilt.

Was this the legendary sleep paralysis?

The only part of my whole body that could still move was my eyeballs, darting alertly to every corner of the room.

In the dark of night, I saw a tall, human-like shadow appear at the doorway of my bedroom.

He was soaked from head to toe, looking like a fish just hauled out of the water, radiating a damp, fishy stench.

Even more terrifyingly, I felt the temperature inside the room plummet rapidly, to the point where even the heated brick bed grew cold.

He walked toward me slowly, and I finally made out his face. His facial features were an exact match to the man in the black-and-white photograph.

It was Zhang Dezhu! [2]

Zhang Dezhu’s skin was shriveled up like a crumpled piece of paper, and water streamed down his trouser legs onto the floor, gathering into a shallow puddle.

*Drip, drop, drip, drop...*

I used every ounce of my strength, but I couldn't even lift a hand, forced to watch helplessly as he drew closer and closer.

"Hehe... did you think that by not opening the door for me, I wouldn't be able to get in?"

Zhang Dezhu's tone turned abruptly sinister and vicious. "Lin Jianlu, you're the one who ruined me. I died in your place, give me back my life!"

*Died in my place?*

But I hadn't done anything!

Suddenly, I thought of what Granny had said in front of the shrine tonight...

I desperately wanted to ask him what on earth was going on, but I couldn't open my mouth at all.

Zhang Dezhu stepped right up to my bed, stretched out those water-bloated hands, and lunged toward my neck...

I tightly closed my eyes, but the suffocation I expected never came. Instead, a shrill, piercing shriek rang in my ears.

"Ah..."

I cracked my eyes open just a sliver, and vaguely saw a tall, jade-like figure standing in front of me.

That person had their back to me. From my perspective, I could only make out a black outer robe that trailed on the floor, its shoulders embroidered with lifelike silver dragons. A cascade of ink-black hair spilled down his back, pinned with two longevity braids.

If the moonlight tonight hadn't been so bright, he would have nearly melted into the dark night, exuding an ancient, silent, and aloof dignity.

Tied around his slender, bone-like fingers was an extremely fine silken thread that shimmered faintly in the moonlight, looking much like the string of an ancient zither.

The other end of the string pierced straight through one of Zhang Dezhu's eyeballs, and that bloodcurdling scream had come from Zhang Dezhu's mouth...

"Stay away from her!" The man's voice was like ice clinking against jade, carrying a faint undercurrent of fury.

Zhang Dezhu seemed utterly terrified of the person before him; his remaining eye filled with panic and cowardice as he shrank back a few paces.

Yet the man was still unsatisfied, scolding Zhang Dezhu as if he were nothing more than an ant, "Get lost!"

Zhang Dezhu shivered violently and actually vanished from my room entirely.

After that, the man turned around. I instinctively looked up at his face...

What met my eyes was a strikingly handsome bone structure. His jawline was ruthlessly sharp, and his features, carved as if from cold jade, were exquisite and profound.

A faint, crimson dot lingered between his brows, adding a vibrant splash of bewitching beauty to his otherwise cold and detached face.

Like a red plum blossom in the snow, passionate yet freezing cold.

When I had seen his hand earlier, I thought this person looked somewhat familiar.

It wasn't until I clearly saw the cinnabar mole between his eyebrows that those lingering, shattered memories from my dreams rushed back like a tidal wave.

It was him!

Good grief, the man from my wet dreams had come to life!

He had crawled out of his coffin to find me...

***

chapters.title: Open
chapters.content:
"Who on earth are you?" I blurted out the question in my heart.

"My name is Long Mingyuan," his tone was utterly indifferent. "Didn't you see me a long time ago?"

That crisp, clear voice was exceptionally familiar, dragging me back to the memory of countless lingering, intimate nights, and my cheeks instantly burned red.

Who would have thought that one day, the object of my erotic dreams would actually appear alive before me!

This was simply too humiliating...

I secretly sized up Long Mingyuan. I had to admit, he was the best-looking person I had ever seen in my life. All those idol celebrities on TV paled into absolute insignificance compared to him.

Pity that this Long Mingyuan exuded an unapproachable indifference in every aspect, like year-round unmelting frost upon a high peak, completely unlike the passionate and obsessive version of him in my dreams.

Yet I was certain: he was the man who had entwined with me in my dreams every night until dawn...

Long Mingyuan gazed at me deeply. His eyes, resembling the blue ice of Lake Baikal, concealed emotions so intense they terrified me.

"Lin Jianlu, I've finally waited for you..."

He raised his hand, as if wanting to touch my face.

Suddenly, I found I could move. I forcefully slapped his hand away and curled up into the corner of the bed.

Long Mingyuan lowered his eyelashes, masking a trace of forbearance in his eyes that I couldn't quite decipher.

I asked vigilantly, "What on earth is going on here?"

He pulled his hand back, saying indifferently, "Your fate is plagued by a tribulation; you were fated not to survive past the second day of the second lunar month this year. But to save you, your grandmother forcibly altered your Eight Characters." [3]

"You can alter the Eight Characters?" I was astonished.

"It is an ancient witchcraft known only to the most prestigious shamans of the Shamanic religion. However, the process is extremely difficult. Even with your grandmother exhausting every skill she had, she only managed to alter your Year Pillar." [4]

Long Mingyuan's ice-blue eyes had returned to calm, unrippled depths. "Except for the Year Pillar, all four pillars of Zhang Dezhu's Eight Characters matched yours. The thing that wanted your life was fooled by your grandmother's illusion, and consequently targeted Zhang Dezhu instead. It was equivalent to him blocking this calamity for you.

"However, Zhang Dezhu died an unnatural death, carrying unappeasable resentment. If he wasn't laid to rest as quickly as possible, he would absorb even more malevolent energy from the world and transform into a malevolent ghost..."

Among the world's seven sins and eight sufferings, greed, hatred, ignorance, arrogance, love, evil, and desire; birth, old age, sickness, death, resentment, and the pain of parting from loved ones, every single one could spawn malevolent energy.

At the burial, Mother Zhang's weeping at the graveside had instead allowed Zhang Dezhu to absorb a great deal of malevolent energy, enough for him to transform into a vengeful spirit.

As night fell, he had come to claim my life...

Thinking of this, I felt as though a basin of ice water had been dumped over me from head to toe, and my teeth began to chatter.

Long Mingyuan seemed to sense my fear, softening his tone considerably. "Don't be afraid. I just chased him down to the netherworld; he won't come pestering you ever again."

His voice possessed a strange, calming power that soothed my taut nerves and lowered my heart rate. I immediately asked, "Who was that thing that wanted my life?"

"It is a malevolent flood dragon sealed by you in the river," he said in a slow, deep tone. "The millennium limit has arrived, and the seal is beginning to loosen. The flood dragon's consciousness is also gradually waking up, which is why it lured Zhang Dezhu to the riverside..."

I could hardly believe my ears, feeling a mix of panic and helplessness in my heart.

It turned out Granny's words were all true, in my past life, I had sealed a malevolent flood dragon with my blood, and now it had come looking for revenge!

All these bizarre and strange events were targeted squarely at me...

No wonder Granny had said to the gods that it was all her fault.

That malevolent flood dragon wanted my life, and Zhang Dezhu... had become my scapegoat!

Sensing my guilt, Long Mingyuan casually remarked, "Don't overthink it. Everything has been predestined long ago. Zhang Dezhu blocked this disaster for you because his own life had reached its end anyway, the outcome is the same, why blame yourself?"

That may have been easy to say, but I still felt like I owed Zhang Dezhu something. I'd better burn him some more paper money later.

After a long silence, I cautiously tested the waters, "Are you the Dragon King of this river?"

At the mention of "Dragon King," a murky, unfathomable look flashed in the depths of Long Mingyuan's eyes.

He didn't answer. Instead, he raised his hand, and a diamond-shaped piece of black jade materialized in his palm.

"Keep this safe. Carry it with you at all times; it can protect you in times of crisis."

My intuition told me that Long Mingyuan had no intention of harming me.

Therefore, I crept over on tiptoe, took the piece of black jade from his palm, and examined it closely.

The black jade felt slightly cool to the touch, refracting a colorful sheen, and its edges were lined with a ring of razor-sharp backward-facing teeth.

Call it black jade, but touching it felt more like scaling a giant creature...

I hesitated. "This is... a protective talisman?"

Aside from opening courier packages, how else was this supposed to protect me?

Long Mingyuan's expression remained as cold and stern as frost. "Your tribulation is not yet over, you cannot let your guard down. Remember, do not go to the Dragon King temple at the head of the village, and do not go near the riverbank! As long as you get through this year, you will be safe for the rest of your life."

What he said matched Granny's warnings. But with so many things already happening before the first lunar month had even ended, how could anyone hope to get through an entire year in peace?

I lowered my head, turning the piece of black jade over in my hands. Out of the corner of my eye, I caught sight of him turning toward the door, and called out, "Long Mingyuan, will I ever see you again?"

Long Mingyuan paused in his tracks, the muscles along his jawline tightening. "No."

"I mean... will I still dream of you in the future?"

The words tumbled out, making my face burn red, as if I were desperately yearning to meet him in my dreams every night.

"No," his tone was resolute, though the tail end of his voice trembled slightly. "If possible, I hope this is the last time we ever meet..."

Hearing this, a sharp pain pierced my heart, and an inexplicable wave of sorrow enveloped me.

I gazed at his lonely, ethereal back, and a stray tear slipped uncontrollably from the corner of my eye.

It felt like reluctance, but even more like heartache.

It was as if I had known him since a very long time ago.

Yet I had only just seen his face clearly today, only just learned his name; why would I have such a strange feeling?

Long Mingyuan left behind a soft parting remark, "Stay obediently by your grandmother's side, she will protect you."

With that, his silhouette dissolved into the hazy, dim light...

"Hey!"

I reached out to grab the hem of his robe, only to jolt awake, sitting straight up in bed.

The room was as normal as ever, and there were no puddles of water on the floor.

Could everything that just happened have been just another dream?

Yet a faint trace of ambergris lingering in the air reminded me that Long Mingyuan's appearance seemed very real.

Just as my confusion mounted, my palm pressed down against a hard, sharp object, nearly cutting my hand.

I picked the object up to look; it was precisely the piece of black jade Long Mingyuan had given me.

***

[1] *Kang*: A traditional northern Chinese brick sleeping platform that can be heated from underneath.

[2] *Note: The raw text renders this name as "Zhang Dezhuzhu" in ch 8; it has been normalized to Zhang Dezhu throughout.*

[3] *Eight Characters (Bazi)*: The Four Pillars of Destiny used in Chinese astrology, consisting of the year, month, day, and hour of birth, each represented by two characters.

[4] *Year Pillar*: The two characters representing the year of one's birth within the Bazi system.

chapters.title: Gold in the Sea
chapters.content:
The next day, I woke up from my warm bed. Remembering what happened last night, my eyes snapped wide open.

This was the first night since my eighteenth birthday that I hadn't had an erotic dream!

If everything Long Mingyuan said was true, does that mean I wouldn't have to experience those dreams ever again?

By the same logic, I would never see Long Mingyuan again either.

This thought made me feel a little buoyant, but deep down, that inexplicable sense of sadness surged back once more.

I forced myself not to be affected by this sudden wave of emotion, got up, and began preparing breakfast.

Passing by Granny's bedroom, I found it completely empty.

Had Granny still not returned?

Snow was still drifting outside. Hesitating for a moment, I decided to go to the village chief's house to see what was going on.

The village chief's daughter-in-law had been in labor all night; why hadn't the baby been born yet?

As soon as I pulled open the large iron gate, I saw Aunt Wang across the way poking her head out, looking over at me.

"Xiaolu, what are you up to this early in the morning?" Aunt Wang asked, exhaling a puff of white vapor.

"My grandmother went to the village chief's house to deliver a baby and still hasn't come back. I need to go check on her," I replied loudly.

Aunt Wang's round, beady eyes darted around, and then she called out, "Xiaolu, come here!"

Full of doubt, I walked over to her side. "Aunt Wang, what is it? Why are you being so secretive..."

Aunt Wang was a rather warm-hearted person. Seeing that Granny and I were lonely and struggling, she often brought us extra vegetables she cooked, and during festivals, she would gift us some fruit and daily necessities.

However, she had also inherited a common trait among rural women in our parts: she loved gossip.

Tucking her hands into her sleeves, she gave me a knowing wink and said, "Xiaolu, do you know why the village chief's young daughter-in-law can't give birth?"

I didn't like gossiping behind people's backs, so I could only play along to humor her. "Why?"

Aunt Wang spat out a sound of disdain. "Isn't it because her son committed too many sins, and retribution has come down on his unborn grandson? I think Heaven purely wants to cut off the village chief's bloodline!"

I awkwardly twitched the corners of my mouth. "Aunt Wang, is it really okay for you to curse the village chief like that?"

"How is that me cursing him?" Aunt Wang glared at me. "That young daughter-in-law, Liu Yazhizhi, has been married to our village for five years, right? She couldn't get pregnant at all, until the village chief's wife found some folk remedy for her from somewhere, and she finally conceived.

Yet the baby was born prematurely at just eight months, right when the heavy snow blocked the mountains, no one can get in or out. Isn't this Heaven's will?

This morning, word has already spread all over the village that Liu Yazhi gave birth to a stillborn baby!"

"What? The baby died?!" I was startled.

"It stopped breathing the moment it came out, all blue and purple... If I were you, I wouldn't go. It's the New Year, bad luck!"

As Aunt Wang spoke, she even fanned the air in front of her with her hand, as if she truly felt the presence of bad luck.

The baby actually died? Could it be that Granny's spell-casting had failed?

But Granny had never had any issues when healing people or seeing fortunes before!

Aunt Wang dug a handful of candied chestnuts out of her pocket and said while chewing, "As for this matter, you really can't blame your grandmother. If you want to blame someone, blame the village chief's son for committing too many sins!"

"Didn't Big Brother Tian take on a lot of construction projects? Building bridges and roads, that's great accumulated merit!" I was deeply puzzled.

The village chief's son was named Tian Hongwei, one of the few college graduates in our village.

After graduation, he worked at the housing and urban-rural development bureau in our town. Later, once he figured out the ropes, he wanted to strike out on his own.

At first, lacking experience, he couldn't get any good projects and was so poor he couldn't even afford meals, having to rely on Liu Yazhi's natal family for relief.

That year, the city wanted to build a cross-river bridge. No one knew what went wrong, but every time the bridge piers were built, they would be washed away by the floodwaters, and the project was delayed for several months without progress.

Tian Hongwei happened to know the chief engineer of that project, and upon hearing about it, he volunteered to join. In less than two months, the cross-river bridge was actually completed.

Later, he became famous because of this bridge, and he took on more and more projects, all of them relatively high-tech engineering works, earning him more and more money.

The fellow villagers all praised the village chief for having a good son, and the village chief's Western-style multi-story house was built higher and higher.

When other people celebrated the New Year, they would take apart their old cotton-padded jackets and replace them with new fabric to make "new" clothes.

Only the village chief's wife wore a brand-new mink fur coat, with a bright gold bracelet dangling from her wrist, making everyone else green with envy.

"Great merit... more like monstrous evil!" Aunt Wang chuckled derisively upon hearing this. "The reason Tian Hongwei was able to build that bridge is because everything he did was wicked and undermined his own virtue! Do you know what 'driving living piles' is?"

As luck would have it, I actually did...

The term "driving living piles" originated from the forbidden book *Lu Ban Jing* (The Classic of Lu Ban). That book not only recorded ancient construction methods but also involved bizarre secret arts such as Taoism, spells, and magic.

Old Master Lu believed that building bridges, embankments, and the like would inevitably disrupt the local *fengshui* and anger the deities, which was why bizarre accidents always occurred during construction.

For example, newly built bridge piers would inexplicably be washed away by water, or mountain road landslides would crush construction workers to death...

The book recorded that if one were building a small path or a small house, slaughtering chickens and sheep as sacrifices would suffice.

However, if the project was massive, like a cross-sea bridge or a mountain-crossing highway, it would inevitably alter the local *fengshui* and fortune, requiring living souls for suppression.

This secret method was called "driving living piles," also known as Lu Ban piles.

During the Republic of China era, there was a major warlord in Guangdong named Chen Jitang, who deeply revered Old Master Lu.

It was rumored that when he was building the Haizhu Bridge, he tied a pair of young boys and girls to the piles and sank them to the bottom of the river.

A century was approaching, and the Haizhu Bridge still stood tall over the Pearl River.

But rumors were rumors after all; they couldn't be taken as truth.

Now that Aunt Wang suddenly brought up the matter of driving living piles, it sent a series of chills down my spine.

"Aunt Wang, do you mean... the reason Big Brother Tian was able to build the cross-river bridge is because he drove living piles?"

Aunt Wang handed me a handful of roasted chestnuts and said in a low voice, "Back then, my old man worked on a project under Tian Hongwei and saw with his own eyes Tian Hongwei push a drunk worker from the construction crew right off the riverbank...

He sneaked into Tian Hongwei's dormitory and dug out some cinnabar and yellow paper used for drawing talismans.

Under the pillow, he also found a cowhide notebook densely written with the birth dates and times of everyone on the construction crew. For every person who met with an accident, he had circled their name with a red cinnabar brush!

Later, as long as it was a project Tian Hongwei was involved in, my old man refused to go no matter what.

Men, you see, once they get rich they turn bad, and Tian Hongwei is cut from the exact same dog's cloth!

Ever since he made a fortune through these crooked ways, he started living the high life, and even kept a female college student in the provincial capital as his mistress. In recent years, he rarely even comes home..."

After listening, I was filled with absolute shock.

Who would have thought that even in this new era, someone would still use such dark and evil secret arts to make a fortune!

No wonder Aunt Wang's attitude was so fierce.

***

chapters.title: Fire in the Furnace
chapters.content:
"Thank you, Aunt Wang, but I still have to go to the village chief's house and bring Granny back." I got up to leave.
